children.author: brudgers
children.text:
The odds that the people who hate everything in the space will love your product are close to zero.

Particularly when what they hate is paying.

If you want to stay in business, customers who want you to stay in business are much much much better than competing on price.

Consumer CAD has a long history and the absence of good products in the space is a consequence of its economic viability.

For context, I’ve been involved with CAD since 1989. I’ve seen many things come and go.

Or, capture the hobbyist and DIY market. Lots of people have 3D printers now. Lots of people hate the existing CAD offerings and especially the fact that the affordable offerings tie you to a cloud service. A product like this is very welcome.
If it is a B2B product, price it like a B2B product so you canbuild a B2B company with B2B service.

That’s fair, and it’s the right thing to weigh with any new tool. Right now it’s a small company and I’ve written most of the engine. What I’ve tried to make sure is that your work never depends on Aircad surviving. Everything exports to DWG, DXF, PDF, and STEP whenever you want, and you can keep native files locally, so the exit path is always open. The engine also runs entirely in your browser, not on our servers. I’d rather earn trust over time than ask for it up front.
As a related note, reading lots of "I built" here is not confidence inspiring, no matter how good you are. There's always that bus factor thing.

OCCT doesn’t handle “complete” fillet/chamfer, right? Where the operation replaces the top line?

Thanks for asking. Core ops are OCCT. It's got great primitives and tolerant modeling. For performance purposes, I've implemented my own algorithms for hidden line rendering, tessellation, and others. I've spent my whole career (15 years+) working on and around kernels.

More detail for the curious: it’s C++ compiled to WebAssembly and runs entirely client-side with a WebGL2 renderer, so there’s no server round-trip for geometry. OCCT does booleans, fillets, and STEP. I replaced its mesher with my own tessellator because BRepMesh was the bottleneck at scale, and hidden-line/Make2D are custom too. Happy to go deeper on any of it.

children.author: mristroph
peetle
children.text:
Thanks so much! That’s basically my favorite thing to hear. :) We spent a ton of time ironing out the bottlenecks for huge projects. CAD users are notorious for pushing products as hard as possible. A few things we did:

The C++/WASM engine owns the model, selection and WebGL2 renderer on one thread, so nothing is copied back and forth on every edit. We use multithreading, SIMD, the works...

For instance, we wrote our own tessellator to replace OpenCASCADE’s mesher, and it only re-meshes the faces that changed. A plate with 2,500 holes meshes in 127 ms instead of about 10 s.

Solids are batched into a few draw calls, and repeated geometry is instanced automatically.

We hunt down anything quadratic. If I had to guess, that is what makes most CAD software interaction slow.
Just checked it out; the whole experience is incredibly smooth.

children.text: Solidworks have a "for makers" product if you're not doing this professionally that has integrated CAM (assuming you don't need 4/5 axis support). It's not free but it's very cheap. If it worked on Linux I'd probably be using it.
This is reasonable criticism of Fusion, but I stick with it for the integrated CAM. Can't really find any other easy to use "professional" caliber software with CAD & CAM at that price.

Fusion is arguably the easiest and best free option to pick up, yet I would urge people to avoid it. No linux support, won't work with any workarounds, mostly online, with the non-CAD part of the UI being absolutely horrible and slow.  
Oh you want to add a new project? Let me animated from the bottom of a hundred of other projects laggily, then wait 5 seconds to be able to name the project, only for it to animate all the way down again!

Onshape, which is also free and runs in the browser, is probably the better choice. This looks more similar to an autocad style drafting application, which isn't an ideal fit for most 3D printing applications. This app is ideal for doing things like architectural work, or traditional machining where the 2D drafts are vital for sharing with the engineers who will actually make the part on a lathe or whatever.

3D printing doesn't need 2D drafts so you're usually better with a solid modelling CAD app. Fusion360, Solidworks and Onshape are all reasonable choices for this - I use onshape because I dislike fusion and solidworks doesn't work on Linux.

Truly nice stuff. I've been looking into getting into 3-d printing recently and wondering could this output the kind of files I could use for that? Truly possibly a noob question, but just wondering if this could do that.

children.text:
Not to brag too much, but I believe that my own code CAD language, Aetheris' Firmament, is a bit ahead of KCL in terms of language design, so maybe take a look and see if Firmament is a better target for you to map to?

https://github.com/yuechen-li-dev/Aetheris/blob/master/fixtu...

That's awesome. I'm also working on a new B-Rep kernel for my own modelling app.

It's small, ~2MB, but already handles a lot of complex modelling and has constraint-based sketching - I'm focusing on watertight shapes for 3D printing, not exact accuracy. All operations map to KCL (KittyCad - now Zoo) so it's possible to edit the code directly.

Might be worth exchanging notes at some point :)

Figure I try pitching at least, but would you consider evaluating my Aetheris kernel to use as Aircad's geometry kernel over OCCT?

https://github.com/yuechen-li-dev/Aetheris

There are currently a lot of newer browser CAD projects that already wraps OCCT WASM, like FluidCAD and Chili3D. And as you said previously, current CAD tools are slow to improve, and part of the reason is because of using kernels first built in the 1980s, and projects like Shapr3D and Plasticity both hit limitations of their existing kernels and switched to Parasolid when their project got bigger, and OCCT's per entity tolerance issue is pretty well know by now.

On another topic, getting a plate with thousands of holes to mesh in under a second is some serious performance, and I do agree with your conclusion that most CAD apps are slow not because of programming language but because accurate NURBS math is inherently slow, but their is also the issues with the 2D constraint solver and fillet/boolean algorithms too. Happy to talk more about the geometry kernel stuff too.

children.author: akadeepesh
children.text: Browser-based CAD with real professional-grade capabilities is a big deal. Especially the scripting API + AI integration that's a much more interesting direction than simply adding an AI chatbot to existing tools. Great work!

source.text:
Aircad is a professional CAD system running in the browser with deep AI integration. It includes professional grade drafting and documentation tools, NURBS-based solid modeling, and a lot more. You can make professional quality design documents with it. It is all integrated behind a scripting API that can do anything you can do in the interface and also perform complex modeling operations efficiently. It reads and writes file formats like DXF, DWG, STEP, and 3DM.

I built Aircad because I was frustrated with what was out there. Current CAD tools are expensive and slow to improve. New features barely move the needle. With Aircad, you have fast, powerful geometry tools for just about anything, from conceptual models to your final design.

The newer generation of web-based CAD isn’t comprehensive enough to complete a project or is slower than existing desktop products because it sends performance-sensitive work to a server (OnShape), or isn’t designed to scale to real work in a collaborative setting (many "toy" CAD tools).

Current CAD collaboration workflows are fragile, costly, and complex. They’re file-based and separate the design artifacts (eg PDFs) from the source. Collaboration is often an expensive add-on that raises your subscription, is hard to learn, and feels unnatural. Aircad builds it in: version history, drawing comparison, forking, and realtime collaboration.

AI in most CAD tools is tacked on as a plug-in instead of being deeply integrated, and those plug-ins are often inefficient, hard to adopt, and costly. Aircad has a built-in AI agent and a comprehensive scripting API with a stage-and-commit workflow, so you know exactly what is happening during a complex change. You can use AI to write new scripts and commands that extend Aircad with repeatable, shareable workflows.
source.title: Show HN: Aircad – Professional drafting and 3D modeling in the browser
